applications.summary: Order API for the ACME web shop: customers (via the storefront) or other systems call it to look up, create and cancel orders, and creating an order charges the customer through Stripe (apps/api/app/routers/orders.py:13-34, apps/api/app/services/order_service.py:25-33). It also fronts the rest of the system: caching order status in Redis, publishing an order-created event to Kafka, and calling a shipping partner (apps/api/app/services/order_service.py:31-42).
responsibilities: Expose HTTP endpoints to look up, create and cancel orders (apps/api/app/routers/orders.py:13-34)
Charge the customer via Stripe as part of order creation (apps/api/app/services/order_service.py:28)
Persist orders to PostgreSQL through a repository layer (apps/api/app/repositories/order_repository.py:11-21, apps/api/app/db.py:8-9)
Cache order status in Redis and publish order-created events to Kafka (apps/api/app/services/order_service.py:31,36-39)
Call the shipping partner API to request shipments (apps/api/app/services/order_service.py:41-42)

applications.summary: The customer-facing storefront: a single-page React app that lets a shopper view their orders by calling acme-api over HTTP (apps/web/src/App.tsx:5-14, apps/web/src/api/client.ts:13-21). It has no backend logic or data store of its own — everything it shows comes from acme-api.
responsibilities: Render the storefront UI with client-side routing for order pages (apps/web/src/App.tsx:5-14)
Fetch a customer's orders from acme-api over HTTP (apps/web/src/api/client.ts:13-16)
Mount the React app into the page (apps/web/src/main.tsx:1-5)
Show an inline error state when a request fails (apps/web/src/components/OrderList.tsx:10,13)

applications.summary: Background job that reacts to orders once acme-api has created them: a Kafka consumer turns each order-created event into a Celery task that computes an invoice reference and files it in S3 (apps/worker/worker/consumer.py:12-16, apps/worker/worker/tasks.py:18-23, apps/worker/worker/storage.py:9-12). It also exposes a nightly reconciliation task against the payment provider, though that task is currently an empty stub (apps/worker/worker/tasks.py:26-29).
responsibilities: Consume ORDER_CREATED events from Kafka and dispatch them as Celery tasks (apps/worker/worker/consumer.py:12-16)
Fulfil orders: compute an invoice reference and store the invoice in S3 (apps/worker/worker/tasks.py:19-22, apps/worker/worker/storage.py:9-12)
Run a nightly reconciliation task against the payment provider, currently unimplemented (apps/worker/worker/tasks.py:26-29)
Own the Celery app/broker configuration for background work (apps/worker/worker/tasks.py:14)

applications.summary: Shared Python library with no runtime of its own: it defines the Order/OrderLine data model and the Kafka event names/contracts that both acme-api and acme-worker import, so the two services agree on the same order shape and event schema (packages/shared/shared/models.py:8-27, packages/shared/shared/events.py:5-16).
responsibilities: Define the Order and OrderLine domain dataclasses used by both services (packages/shared/shared/models.py:8-27)
Define Kafka topic name constants and the OrderCreated event payload contract (packages/shared/shared/events.py:5-16)
Act as the single shared dependency acme-api and acme-worker both import from (packages/shared/shared/__init__.py:1; apps/api/app/routers/orders.py:5; apps/worker/worker/tasks.py:9-10)

components.summary: The bootstrap/wiring layer of acme-api: builds the FastAPI app and mounts the orders router (apps/api/app/main.py:8-9), owns the raw psycopg2 connection helper (apps/api/app/db.py:8-9), and holds all runtime configuration, including one hardcoded secret and an always-on debug flag (apps/api/app/config.py:5,9).

The entire UI and data-fetching layer of @acme/web: OrderList.tsx renders the order list and an error state, client.ts wraps the axios calls to acme-api, App.tsx defines the routes, and main.tsx mounts the app into the DOM.

A pure domain-contract package: dataclasses for Order/OrderLine (models.py) plus Kafka event-name constants and the OrderCreated payload (events.py) — no logic, no I/O. It declares pydantic as a dependency but nothing in it imports pydantic.

flows.narrative: Triggered by an automated caller (e.g. a load balancer or orchestrator) hitting GET /health. It decides nothing and changes nothing — it returns a hardcoded {"status": "ok"} without checking the database, cache, or Kafka connectivity (apps/api/app/main.py:12-14). What can go wrong: this is a liveness check only, not a readiness check — it can report healthy even while PostgreSQL, Redis or Kafka are unreachable, since none of those are touched in the handler.

Three separate business actions share this router. Create (POST /orders): triggered by a client submitting an order; it only checks that customer_id is present (apps/api/app/routers/orders.py:25-26), builds an Order with no line items from the payload (apps/api/app/routers/orders.py:27), then calls OrderService.create, which unconditionally raises ValueError when order.lines is empty (apps/api/app/services/order_service.py:26-27) — as wired today, POST /orders can never succeed. Lookup (GET /orders/{id}): reads the order from PostgreSQL and 404s if it is missing (apps/api/app/routers/orders.py:14-19) — this path works as intended. Cancel (DELETE /orders/{id}): does not look up or update the order at all; it just echoes back {"cancelled": order_id} without touching the repository or database (apps/api/app/routers/orders.py:31-34), so a customer's order status is unchanged by 'cancelling' it.

Triggered when the Kafka consumer reads an ORDER_CREATED message and calls fulfil_order.delay(order_id) as a Celery task (apps/worker/worker/consumer.py:12-16). It makes no decisions: it derives an MD5-based reference from the order id (apps/worker/worker/tasks.py:21) and stores an 'invoice' object in S3 keyed by order id (apps/worker/worker/storage.py:9-12). What can go wrong: despite the docstring promising to 'mark the order shipped' (apps/worker/worker/tasks.py:20), the function only returns the ORDER_SHIPPED string (apps/worker/worker/tasks.py:23) — it never writes back to PostgreSQL or publishes an event, so no order's stored status actually changes; and if the S3 write fails, the task raises with no visible retry/error handling.

Intended to run on a schedule (task name orders.reconcile) to reconcile a given day's orders against the payment provider, per its own docstring (apps/worker/worker/tasks.py:28). In its current form it triggers no real work: the body is a stub that immediately returns 0 with no Stripe or PostgreSQL calls (apps/worker/worker/tasks.py:26-29). What can go wrong: anyone relying on this task to catch payment/order mismatches is not actually protected — it is a placeholder, not a working reconciliation job.

findings.reasoning: find_orders_by_customer builds SQL with Python %-formatting directly from an unsanitised customer_id (apps/api/app/db.py:14), unlike the parameterised queries used elsewhere in the same codebase (apps/api/app/repositories/order_repository.py:13,19). It is currently dead code — no caller was found anywhere in the scanned source — but customer_id is exactly the kind of value that arrives from a request path/query parameter, so this is a landmine that becomes exploitable the moment it is wired to an endpoint.

request_shipment makes a real outbound HTTPS POST to the configured shipping partner with verify=False (apps/api/app/services/order_service.py:41-42, target URL from apps/api/app/config.py:10), which disables certificate validation and allows a man-in-the-middle to intercept or forge shipment requests. No current router calls this method, but it is a real, exported code path with no test or comment explaining the bypass.

The literal Stripe secret is not unused decoration: it is assigned to stripe.api_key at import time (apps/api/app/services/order_service.py:16), so the key is live and every order-creation call uses it. Anyone who reads this repository (public history included) has a usable payment credential regardless of the 'hardcoded on purpose' comment.

DEBUG is hardcoded True with no environment override, unlike every other setting in the same file (DATABASE_URL, REDIS_URL, KAFKA_BROKERS all read from os.getenv, apps/api/app/config.py:6-8), and it is wired straight into FastAPI's debug=True (apps/api/app/main.py:8), so the app ships with debug mode on in every environment, including production.

The Dockerfile does set ENV DEBUG=1, but the application never reads that environment variable — apps/api/app/config.py:5 hardcodes DEBUG = True directly with no os.getenv call, unlike DATABASE_URL/REDIS_URL/KAFKA_BROKERS in the same file. So this specific line has no effect on runtime behaviour today; the real, active cause of debug mode is apps/api/app/config.py:5. Worth cleaning up as dead/misleading configuration, but fixing it alone would not turn debug mode off.

The value injected is String(e) from a caught axios/network failure (apps/web/src/components/OrderList.tsx:10), not raw response body or user input, so under the current call path (apps/web/src/api/client.ts:13-16) the rendered text is normally a generic message like 'AxiosError: ...' rather than attacker-controlled HTML — exploitability today is low. It remains a fragile pattern: if acme-api's error responses ever get echoed into that string (e.g. a future change surfaces e.response.data), this becomes a real stored/reflected-in-UI XSS.

MD5 here is not used for passwords, signatures, or any integrity/authentication decision — it only derives an arbitrary reference string that gets written as the body of an S3 object (apps/worker/worker/tasks.py:21-22, apps/worker/worker/storage.py:9-11). MD5's collision weakness has no security consequence in this usage, though a UUID or SHA-256 would be cleaner practice.

This bind only runs inside the container entrypoint (apps/api/pyproject.toml:19 wires 'acme-api = app.main:main'; apps/api/Dockerfile:6-7 EXPOSE 8080 and CMD run uvicorn the same way). Binding 0.0.0.0 is required for the service to be reachable from other containers/the host in this docker-compose setup (docker-compose.yml maps '8080:8080' to the api service) — binding to localhost would break the intended deployment, not secure it.

diagrams.caption: Shows who and what surrounds this system — end users, a scheduler, and the eight outside services it talks to (Stripe, Kafka, AWS, PostgreSQL and more) — without showing any code detail, so the reader can see this is a small system with a surprisingly large number of outside dependencies.

Shows the four buildable pieces of software (the order API, the storefront, the worker, and the shared library) as boxes, with arrows to each other and to the outside services each one uses, making clear that only the storefront is a user-facing app and everything else is backend order-processing plumbing.

Shows, inside each application, which internal code folders depend on which others, and makes visible that most folders lean on the shared library while a small cluster of folders inside the API depend on each other in a loop that would be harder to change one piece at a time.

Shows the four applications side by side with lines to each other and to the outside systems they use, making clear that the shared library is a hub used by both backend services while the storefront only ever talks to the order API, never directly to a database or payment provider.

Lists every outside service, database, cache and queue this small codebase talks to (eight in total, including Stripe for payment and PostgreSQL for orders), so the reader can see how many outside things could break this system if any one of them goes down.

Shows how the code is packaged to run — three Dockerfiles, six services wired together with docker-compose, and the Terraform that provisions the cloud database and storage bucket — so the reader can see everything is meant to be run together as containers, the same locally as in the cloud.

insights.title: Three biggest risks: a broken create-order path, an untransactional payment flow, and committed secrets/TLS bypass
insights.detail: 1) POST /orders can never complete — order.lines is never populated from the request payload (apps/api/app/routers/orders.py:27) and OrderService.create unconditionally rejects an order with no lines (apps/api/app/services/order_service.py:26-27); fix this first, it blocks the core business function entirely. 2) Stripe is charged before the order is saved, cached or published (apps/api/app/services/order_service.py:28-32), so any downstream failure leaves a paid order that was never recorded, with no working reconciliation job to catch it (apps/worker/worker/tasks.py:26-29 is a stub). 3) A live Stripe secret is hardcoded and wired into the SDK (apps/api/app/config.py:9, apps/api/app/services/order_service.py:16) and outbound shipping calls disable TLS verification (apps/api/app/services/order_service.py:42) — both ship inside the built Docker image.

insights.title: Tacit conventions a newcomer would need to learn
insights.detail: The shared package is imported as top-level `shared`, not by its folder path — `from shared.events import ...` / `from shared.models import Order` (apps/api/app/routers/orders.py:5, apps/worker/worker/tasks.py:9-10) — because packages/shared is installed as an editable dependency named acme-shared/shared, which is not obvious from the directory layout alone. Inside acme-api there is a real circular import between app, app/repositories, app/routers and app/services (app imports app/routers at apps/api/app/main.py:6, app/repositories imports app at apps/api/app/repositories/order_repository.py:5, app/services imports app/repositories and is imported by app/routers) even though the code reads like a clean controller/service/repository layering. Most config values are environment-driven (apps/api/app/config.py:6-8) but DEBUG is a hardcoded literal with no env override (apps/api/app/config.py:5) — a pattern a newcomer could easily miss and 'fix' incorrectly by only touching the Dockerfile. There are no tests anywhere in the repo despite pytest and vitest being declared as dev dependencies (apps/api/pyproject.toml:16, apps/web/package.json:19,21), and no npm lockfile is committed, so a fresh `npm install` is not reproducible.

insights.title: What breaks if each external system goes down
insights.detail: PostgreSQL down: every order read/write fails (apps/api/app/repositories/order_repository.py:11-21) — no fallback, a hard single point of failure for all order data. Stripe down: order creation is blocked entirely, since the charge is the first thing OrderService.create does (apps/api/app/services/order_service.py:28) — no queueing or deferred billing. Redis down: cache.set after a successful charge+save would raise (apps/api/app/services/order_service.py:31), turning an already-completed, already-charged order into a failed-looking request with no compensating cleanup. Kafka down: publish() after payment+save would raise (apps/api/app/services/order_service.py:36-39), and separately the worker's consumer can't receive ORDER_CREATED at all (apps/worker/worker/consumer.py:12-13) — orders stay paid but unfulfilled, with no other trigger for fulfilment. AWS S3 down: fulfil_order's store_invoice call fails with no visible error handling (apps/worker/worker/storage.py:9-12, apps/worker/worker/tasks.py:22), blocking invoice generation. Celery/broker down: no worker task can be dispatched or executed at all (apps/worker/worker/tasks.py:14). shipping.acme-logistics.example down: no current effect, since nothing in the scanned code calls request_shipment yet (apps/api/app/services/order_service.py:41-42). Overall single point of failure: the order-creation request path chains Stripe, PostgreSQL, Redis and Kafka synchronously with no retry/circuit-breaker (apps/api/app/services/order_service.py:25-33), so any one of those four failing during that one request can leave a customer charged with no matching order record.

insights.title: shipping.acme-logistics.example is real integration code, but currently unreached
insights.detail: This is not an incidental mention — config.py defines the real base URL (apps/api/app/config.py:10) and order_service.py has a working method that POSTs to it (apps/api/app/services/order_service.py:41-42). However, no router or other entrypoint in the scanned code calls request_shipment, so this integration is currently dead code from the perspective of the running API: it exists and is wired to real config, but nothing invokes it yet.

insights.title: Creating an order can never succeed as the code is wired today
insights.detail: POST /orders builds an Order with no line items from the request payload (apps/api/app/routers/orders.py:27), and OrderService.create unconditionally raises ValueError when order.lines is empty (apps/api/app/services/order_service.py:26-27). Every call to the only order-creation endpoint therefore throws an unhandled exception, which FastAPI turns into a 500 rather than the intended validation response. This is the single biggest functional risk in the repo and would be the first thing to fix — either populate lines from the payload in the router, or relax/rework the validation in OrderService.

insights.title: Payment is charged before the order is durably saved, with no compensating transaction
insights.detail: OrderService.create calls stripe.Charge.create before self.repository.save(order), and before the Redis cache write and Kafka publish that follow it (apps/api/app/services/order_service.py:28-32). If the database write, Redis write, or Kafka publish fails after a successful charge, the customer has been billed but there is no order record and no downstream fulfilment event — a lost, unrecoverable paid order with no retry or reconciliation path (the worker's reconcile task is itself an unimplemented stub, see apps/worker/worker/tasks.py:26-29).

insights.title: Committed Stripe secret and disabled TLS verification ship in the API's Docker image
insights.detail: A live Stripe secret key is hardcoded and wired directly into the Stripe SDK at import time (apps/api/app/config.py:9, apps/api/app/services/order_service.py:16), and outbound calls to the shipping partner skip certificate validation (apps/api/app/services/order_service.py:42). Both ship as-is inside apps/api/Dockerfile, meaning the built image and the git history both carry a usable payment credential and a network path open to interception.

insights.title: DELETE /orders/{order_id} does not touch the database
insights.detail: cancel_order returns {"cancelled": order_id} without calling the repository or checking that the order exists (apps/api/app/routers/orders.py:31-34). Callers get a 200 response, but the order's stored status is unchanged, so any code or reporting that trusts the order's status column after a 'cancel' call will be wrong.

insights.title: GET /health is a liveness check, not a readiness check
insights.detail: The handler returns a hardcoded {"status": "ok"} without checking PostgreSQL, Redis, or Kafka connectivity (apps/api/app/main.py:12-14), even though the reconstructed process flow implies it touches those systems. An orchestrator relying on this endpoint would consider the service healthy even if its database or broker were unreachable.

insights.title: fulfil_order never updates persisted order status or publishes ORDER_SHIPPED
insights.detail: The task's docstring says it will 'mark the order shipped' (apps/worker/worker/tasks.py:20), but the function only returns the ORDER_SHIPPED string constant (apps/worker/worker/tasks.py:23) — it never writes to PostgreSQL or publishes an event for any other consumer to observe, so no order's status actually changes as a result of fulfilment.
